title: Attachment to people
tomorrow: Simran's college email arrives. why does Bebe ask, thank who?

cards: Bebe is walking without the boot now, slowly, with a cane. At dinner she sets down her spoon and announces it: next Sunday she's going home, to her own house and her chilies. Simran's dad nods.
Bhua Kiran says she'll stay the first few nights. Simran stands up so fast her chair scrapes. She's been the one sleeping on the couch, driving to therapy, fetching the glasses.
You can't, she says. What if you fall again? Who'll hear you?
Bebe looks at her for a long moment, and then asks: putt, are you keeping me safe, or keeping me?

teach.b: That's exactly the question Gurbani asks about moh. The love isn't the problem. Simran's love for Bebe is real, and the Gurus never ask anyone to love less.
The problem is the clutch: the grip that wants someone to stay put so we don't have to feel afraid.
Guru Arjan, on ang 1358, pictures moh as a warrior who wins even against the strong, and this is how it wins: it looks exactly like care.

teach.h: ANG 938: THE LOTUS IN THE WATER.
teach.b: Guru Nanak gives another picture, on ang 938, in the Sidh Gosht, in paraphrase: live like the lotus that stays untouched in the water, like the duck that swims in the stream and comes out dry.

The lotus is in the water, rooted in it, not drowned by it. That's love without clutch: fully in the relationship, and not pulling the other person under with you. A grip says the other person's choices are ours to make.
Love says their life is still theirs, even when we're scared.

teach.h: I'M HERE, NOT YOU CAN'T GO.
teach.b: Here's the line worth repeating: love says I'm here; clutch says you can't go. After dinner, Simran sits next to Bebe and they make a deal. Bebe goes home on Sunday.
Simran will call every evening and come Saturdays to water the chilies.
Bebe laughs her big laugh. Simran, she says, the chilies were never in danger. Then, softer: but thank you for worrying about me.

how: Sikh teaching treats family love as good and householder life as a path to God, while naming moh, possessive attachment, as one of the five thieves; the lotus in water is a familiar image for living in the world without being drowned by it.

o: loving so tightly you won't let them choose
missing a close friend who moved far away
a family's duty to look after its elders

games.q: love without the clutch — tap the pairs.
p: a grip that looks like care
the lotus untouched in the water

s: the Gurus teach that to escape moh you must love your family less
the love isn't the problem; the clutch is. the Gurus never ask anyone to love less.
Guru Nanak's Sidh Gosht pictures the lotus untouched in the water
ang 938: in the water, rooted in it, not drowned.
if you truly love someone, you stop them from taking risks
that's moh at its most convincing: it looks exactly like care.

games.q: your younger brother wants to take the bus across town alone for the first time. you're scared for him. what fits today's line?
o: help him plan the trip, and ask him to text when he's there.
tell your parents to say no until you feel ready.
say nothing and let him figure it out entirely alone.
games.why: love says i'm here; clutch says you can't go. Simran's deal: Bebe goes home, and Simran calls every evening and waters the chilies on Saturdays.

practice: If there's paper near you, write the name of someone you love, and under it one choice that's theirs to make, not yours. If there's no paper, trace the name on your palm with a finger. Then let the hand rest open, and breathe.

wordCard.voice: Attachment to people. Moh dressed up as care, and love that stays close without holding someone in place.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: moh, attachment; today, the grip on a person, which can look exactly like care.

carryVoice: Love, not clutch: like the lotus, in the water and not under it. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Ang 938 (Ramkali, Sidh Gosht, Mahala 1: jaise jal meh kamal niraalam murgaaee nai saane), paraphrased
Ang 1358 (Salok Sahaskriti, Mahala 5: the salok addressed to moh), paraphrased
